blocks.text: Phospholipids play important structural roles in making plasma membranes. Chemically they are the derivatives of phosphatidic acid. Phosphatidic acid is composed of one glycerol, two fatty acids and one phosphoric acid (phosphate). Any nitrogenous base e.g., choline, ethanolamine or serine attaches with its phosphoric acid and makes phospholipid. Common examples are phosphatidyl choline (lecithin), phosphatidyl ethanolamine and phosphatidyl serine. Phosphatidyl choline (Figure 4.35) forms lipid bilayer in plasma membranes.

blocks.alt: Top: the four components with formulas: Glycerol, Fatty acid (HO-C(=O)-Long hydrocarbon chain), Phosphate, Nitrogenous base (Choline). Middle: a phospholipid as a hydrophilic head with two hydrophobic tails. Bottom: the full molecule: choline - phosphate - glycerol with two fatty acids ((CH2)14-CH3 and (CH2)7-CH=CH-(CH2)7-CH3); brackets Phosphatidic acid and Phosphatidyl choline.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.35: Phosphatidyl choline - a phospholipid (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.35).

blocks.text: Phospholipids have two parts of their molecules i.e., head and tail. Head is polar and contains nitrogenous base and phosphate group while tail is non polar and contains the two fatty acids.
